what_its_for: Entacapone is used to treat Parkinson's disease. It works alongside your levodopa/carbidopa medicine to help control the symptoms of Parkinson's disease, such as shaking, stiffness, and slow movement. It helps your levodopa medicine work longer and more smoothly by preventing your body from breaking it down too quickly.
how_to_take: Take entacapone by mouth with or without food. Always take it at the same time as each dose of your levodopa/carbidopa medicine — do not take it separately. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush or chew the tablet. Take it exactly as your doctor prescribed and do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause serious problems.
dosing: The usual dose is one 200 mg tablet taken with EACH dose of your levodopa/carbidopa medicine. Most people take it 3 to 8 times per day, depending on how often they take their levodopa. Your doctor will decide the right number of doses for you. Do not take more than 8 tablets (1,600 mg) in one day unless your doctor tells you to.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if you are also taking your levodopa/carbidopa dose at the same time. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never double up on doses to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store entacapone at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can cause dizziness, drowsiness, or sudden sleepiness. Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this medicine can cause low blood pressure and make you feel dizzy or faint. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can increase drowsiness. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, or supplements you take, as entacapone can interact with certain antidepressants (especially MAO inhibitors), blood thinners like warfarin, and medicines for iron deficiency. Do not take iron supplements at the same time as entacapone — take them at least 2 to 3 hours apart.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: high fever, stiff muscles, confusion, or fast heartbeat (these could be signs of a rare but serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); unusual or uncontrollable movements of your face, arms, or legs; hallucinations or seeing/hearing things that are not there; severe diarrhea or stomach pain; dark brown or black urine (this can be a normal harmless side effect but mention it to your doctor); unusual urges such as gambling, eating, spending money, or increased sexual urges; skin that looks yellow (jaundice); or if you feel very confused, faint, or have trouble breathing. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly — always talk to your doctor first.
when_it_works: Entacapone starts working within about 1 to 2 hours after your first dose. However, you may not notice the full benefit right away. Most people begin to see improvement in their Parkinson's symptoms — such as less 'wearing off' between doses — within the first few days to weeks of starting the medicine. It works best when taken consistently with every dose of your levodopa/carbidopa medicine.
special_populations: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness, confusion, and low blood pressure, so use extra caution. People with liver problems should use entacapone with caution, as it may not be safe — tell your doctor if you have any liver disease. Entacapone is not approved for use in children. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before taking this medicine, as the safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been fully established.
